content:
Arthritis is often thought of as a condition affecting older adults, but in the UK, around 15,000 children and young people are living with arthritis. Understanding the condition and accessing the right support is crucial for managing symptoms and maintaining quality of life.

Quick answer: Arthritis can affect young people, with around 15,000 children and young people in the UK living with the condition. Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) is the most common form in under-16s, causing joint pain, swelling, and stiffness. Symptoms can include morning stiffness, fatigue, and fevers. Early diagnosis by a GP and paediatric rheumatologist is important for managing the condition.

Types of Arthritis in Young People

Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA)

JIA is the most common type of arthritis in under-16s. "Idiopathic" means the cause is unknown. There are several subtypes:

  • Oligoarticular JIA — affects 4 or fewer joints, most common type
  • Polyarticular JIA — affects 5 or more joints
  • Systemic JIA — causes whole-body symptoms including fevers and rash
  • Enthesitis-related JIA — affects where tendons attach to bone
  • Psoriatic JIA — associated with the skin condition psoriasis

Reactive Arthritis

Can develop after an infection and usually resolves within weeks to months.

Young Adult Onset

Rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, and other inflammatory types can begin in the late teens or twenties.

Recognising Symptoms

  • Joint pain, swelling, or stiffness lasting more than 6 weeks
  • Limping or reluctance to use a limb (in younger children)
  • Morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes
  • Fatigue beyond normal tiredness
  • Unexplained fevers with joint symptoms

Getting Diagnosed in the UK

If you suspect arthritis in a child or young person:

  1. See your GP — describe all symptoms and how long they've lasted
  2. Request a referral to a paediatric rheumatologist
  3. NHS waiting times vary — ask about urgent referral if symptoms are severe

UK Support Resources

  • JIGSAW (Joint Involvement Group for Self-Advocacy Workshops)
  • NRAS (National Rheumatoid Arthritis Society) — resources for young people
  • Young people's rheumatology clinics — many NHS trusts run dedicated youth clinics
  • School support — children with JIA may qualify for an EHCP (Education, Health and Care Plan)

Living Well as a Young Person with Arthritis

  • Stay as active as possible — swimming and cycling are excellent
  • Talk to teachers and employers about reasonable adjustments
  • Connect with peers online — social support reduces isolation
  • Transition planning — move from paediatric to adult rheumatology services smoothly

If you're a young person with persistent joint symptoms, don't delay seeking help. Early treatment can prevent joint damage and improve long-term outcomes.

Practical next steps for Arthritis in Young People – UK Guide

If you came here about Arthritis in Young People – UK Guide, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask community musculoskeletal services about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Making information usable

Treat articles like this as a starting map, not a personal care plan. Highlight one idea to try for two weeks, then review. If symptoms are new, rapidly worsening, or affecting several joints with fever or unexplained weight loss, contact your GP promptly rather than waiting on self-help alone.

Building a joint-friendly routine

Start with short sessions you can repeat on most days. Warm water, cycling, or paced walking often suits stiff joints better than sudden high-impact bursts. Increase time or resistance slowly, and leave a rest day when a joint is hot, swollen or unusually painful. If you are unsure where to begin, ask about NHS physiotherapy or an exercise referral scheme via your GP surgery.

Quick questions about Arthritis Young People Guide

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
